source.title: Scaling New Frontiers: Insights into Large Recommendation Models
source.authors: Wei Guo; Hao Wang; Luankang Zhang; Jin Yao Chin; Zhongzhou Liu; Kai Cheng; Qiushi Pan; Yi Quan Lee; Wanqi Xue; Tingjia Shen; Kenan Song; Kefan Wang; Wenjia Xie; Yuyang Ye; Huifeng Guo; Yong Liu; Defu Lian; Ruiming Tang; Enhong Chen

page_placements.theme: Recommendation scaling depends on backbone, history and feature handling

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own model-scaling experiments in recommendation systems, a different model domain from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The experiments vary recommendation-model depth and report recall or ranking metrics. They do not measure held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy, fit or test power laws for loss, test small-run extrapolation, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The recommendation results therefore do not directly measure any listed version; they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study varies transformer depth (2–32 blocks, about one order of magnitude) in recommendation models. It reports recall metrics (HR, NDCG, MRR) and ranking AUC and Logloss. It fits no power law, tests no extrapolation, and examines no compute-optimal parameter/token split. It concerns recommendation models, not language-model pretraining loss. The only held-out loss reported is ranking Logloss across depth, and it is non-monotonic with no functional fit. That cannot show whether V5's power-law form holds outside text pretraining. The results measure a related construct (whether recommendation metrics improve with depth), so they are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as tests. The reader's 'tests/T3' with all versions not_tested is internally inconsistent.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that HSTU and Llama scale with depth in recall while GPT and SASRec do not. Relative attention bias and the residual pattern drive scalability. HSTU scales in multi-domain, multi-behavior and ranking tasks. Model size (depth and embedding width) should be matched to dataset size. Lower Logloss does not always mean better AUC, so scaling laws alone may be insufficient.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates recommendation-model metrics while varying transformer depth and other settings; it does not reproduce language-model held-out loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with architecture, dataset, model depth, side-information inclusion, and (for ranking) metric.

fits_no_version.finding: In recommendation recall, HSTU and Llama metrics rise with depth on ML-20M. GPT and SASRec collapse beyond 2–8 blocks: GPT ML-1M HR@10 falls from 0.2798 to 0.0247.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In sequential recommendation, gains from added transformer depth depend on the backbone; some standard backbones degrade sharply with depth.

fits_no_version.finding: HSTU depth scaling persists when single components are ablated, but plateaus most without relative attention bias. Side information and multi-behavior settings show mostly increasing but non-monotonic trends.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth-scaling of recommendation models depends on specific components such as relative attention bias and residual pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: HSTU improves with depth in multi-domain recall and generally in ranking AUC. Ranking Logloss and AUC disagree across depths, and Llama ranking shows little or negative gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation ranking, reductions in held-out loss do not reliably track ranking-metric gains as depth grows.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 6 (ML-20M) sweeps dim, depth and sequence length. Performance peaks then fluctuates. The authors state the optimal layers × dim product stays roughly constant and grows with sequence length.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation models, the recall-optimal model size (L·D) is bounded by data size and grows with it.

record.problems: The experiments report recommendation metrics rather than held-out language-model loss and do not fit power laws or test extrapolation. No uncertainty estimates are stated. Some scaling evidence is described qualitatively or presented in tables and figures without a consistent power-law analysis.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional per-depth metric values and experiments, including Tables 1–17, Figures 4–5, parameter sweeps, component ablations, multi-behavior comparisons and ranking-condition variations. They are omitted because they concern recommendation metrics rather than a listed claim version; the rows retained summarize representative reported scaling outcomes and key exceptions.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss; no power-law fit against parameters, tokens or compute.
No fit on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens.
No language-model loss at fixed parameter count across shapes. The recommendation dim/depth sweeps use recall metrics.
Recommendation models are trained at several depths, but no power-law form is fitted to loss or metrics.
No downstream task performance of language models related to scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Parameter sweep over embedding dimension, depth and sequence length, with the authors' claim that the optimal L·D is constant and grows with data. Relevant context for V3/V4-type claims, though it uses recall metrics in recommendation.
Smaller item embedding (size 4) changes depth-scaling of ranking AUC: it worsens on ML-20M and improves on smaller datasets.

record.verdict_notes: This is not one of the original sources. No power law is fitted, no compute or token axis is varied, and the depth range is only 2–32 blocks. The paper's use of 'scaling law' means 'metric improves with depth'. Mapping it to V5 would overstate what it shows.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or loss scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger runs is tested.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation or compute-optimal split is tested.
The paper compares architectures and depth, but not architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Recommendation models are evaluated, but the paper does not test whether the same power-law form holds in another modality or training regime.
Recommendation metrics are measured, not downstream performance of language models as predicted by scale or pretraining loss.
The paper reports sensitivity to architecture, dataset and model size in recommendation tasks, but does not compare fitted exponents, parameter-counting choices, or compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Removed one HSTU component at a time and varied block count.
rows.value: The authors report that most ablated models retained scalability; performance plateaued most notably without relative attention bias, especially from 8 to 32 blocks.
rows.note: Qualitative summary of the reported depth sweep; recommendation metrics, not loss.

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Varied block count with and without item side information.
rows.measure: HR@10, HR@50, NDCG@10, NDCG@50 and MRR
rows.value: The authors report that scalability was maintained with side information, while including it usually produced slightly inferior results; the table has non-monotonic values across depths.
rows.note: Aggregate textual report across the two datasets and listed metrics; individual table values are not combined here.
rows.check: The authors say performance 'consistently improves with increased depth', but Table 9 contradicts this in places. For example, ML-1M without side info peaks at 16 blocks: HR@10 is 0.3333 at 16 and 0.3289 at 32. The row's partial state is right; the authors' wording overstates the trend.

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of model layers in multi-behavior experiments.
rows.value: The authors report that overall performance generally improved with layer count, with a few exceptions; they state the trend also held on IJCAI.
rows.note: No numerical values are given in the text for this sweep.

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Varied HSTU block count in multi-domain recommendation.

conditions.value: Digital Music, Movies & TV, Toys, Video Games

rows.value: Performance improves with model complexity across all four domains, according to the authors.
rows.note: The authors particularly note gains in Digital Music and Video Games; this is not a fitted power-law result.

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer block count in ranking experiments.
rows.value: The authors describe HSTU as generally improving with increased depth, while noting that Logloss and AUC can disagree; for example, on ML-1M the 32-block model has higher AUC but worse Logloss than the 24-block model.
rows.note: The text does not claim monotonic improvement for every dataset or metric.
rows.check: Logloss is a held-out loss but is non-monotonic in depth. HSTU on AMZ-Books goes 0.4608, 0.4682, 0.5134, 0.5089, 0.4496, 0.4140. No power-law fit is given, so the row stays linked to none.

rows.subject: Llama
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer block count in ranking experiments.
rows.value: The authors report minimal improvement with increased blocks and slight decreases in some cases.

relation.reason: It discusses power-law scaling and prior HSTU findings, while its own experiments establish recommendation performance trends rather than testing the catalog's claim versions.

tranche.reason: The study measures recommendation scalability with depth and other settings, without testing power-law form, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, fixed-parameter shape invariance, downstream prediction from pretraining, or fitted-law dependence.

source_check.notes: All four endpoint comparisons are accurate. The power-law compute result spanning three orders of magnitude in the introduction is attributed to prior HSTU work, not established by this study.
